design_detail: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42021286619; PRISMA and MOOSE; R metafor) of observational studies comparing positive- and negative-symptom severity between people with methamphetamine-induced psychosis and people with schizophrenia or a related disorder intended to be free of drug use: 12 studies, 624 vs 527 people; standardized mean differences (Hedges' g) from baseline or single-time scores; quality rated with a modified Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Read: all nine pages; Table 1 and Figures 1 to 3 checked on the rendered pages, with the study values of the two forest plots read from the images; supplementary tables S1 to S5 and figures S1 to S12 not read.
can_establish: The average reported difference in positive- and negative-symptom scores between treated clinical groups with methamphetamine psychosis and with schizophrenia, across small samples published to December 2022.
cannot_establish: Whether the two conditions differ at onset or without treatment (most participants were treated and described as stable); whether any difference holds separately for acute and persistent methamphetamine psychosis (mixed in the pools); whether any symptom tells an individual's diagnosis (no diagnostic-accuracy data); and why any difference exists (cross-sectional comparisons).

sample.recruitment: PubMed, Embase and PsycINFO to 16 December 2022 (English, human, ages 18 to 65), with snowball searching of reference lists; 2052 records (pp. 182–183). Included studies came from Japan (3), Taiwan (2), Australia (2), China, Iran, Canada and South Africa (1 each) and one multinational WHO study (Australia, Japan, the Philippines, Thailand); mostly outpatients, five studies with both in- and outpatients (3.2, p. 184).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: observational studies of adults aged 18 to 65 with schizophrenia, schizoaffective or a related disorder by DSM or ICD, and of people currently using methamphetamine or with persistent psychotic symptoms after recent cessation of intoxication or acute withdrawal (within one month), methamphetamine being the primary or only drug. Excluded: reports of current or recent (within two years) use of other substances except tobacco (the text does not say to which group this applies); first-episode psychosis and mood disorders; case reports and qualitative studies (2.4, p. 183). Two studies of acute exacerbation after methamphetamine intake were excluded (Medhus 2013; Tomiyama 1990) (3.1).
sample.demographics: Mean ages 31.35 years (methamphetamine psychosis) and 32.46 years (schizophrenia); men 67.98% and 63.3%, which are unweighted means of the study percentages in Table 1 (editors' check); one study (Zhang 2018) was much younger (means 21.0 and 23.8 years) (3.1; 3.2; Table 1).
sample.attrition: Not applicable: baseline or single-time scores; follow-up data from the cohort and prospective studies were not used.
sample.selection_effects: Treated clinical samples described as stable, with mean antipsychotic doses of about 440 to 1,360 mg/day chlorpromazine equivalents where reported (Table 1); only five studies specified a minimum period of clinical stability (3.2). The methamphetamine-psychosis groups mix persistent psychosis after abstinence, psychosis with current use and lifetime substance-induced psychosis, and comparison groups were not always free of drug use (Hides 2015; Hajebi 2018; see comparison).

exposure.measurement: Diagnosis of methamphetamine-induced or -associated psychosis by DSM-III, DSM-IV(-TR), DSM-5, ICD-10 or the MINI in each study; only one study specified that methamphetamine was the main drug, one reported the dose (Chen 2015), and five the age at first use (3.2, p. 184).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesized; dose reported in one study, route and quality of the drug mostly unreported (4.6, p. 188).
exposure.polysubstance: Six studies reported concomitant use of alcohol, cannabis, cocaine, heroin, MDMA, ketamine, opioids or nicotine and five did not report it (3.2; 4.6); other drug use was not accounted for in the analysis.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Heterogeneous and often unreported (4.6; Supplementary Table S2, not read); some groups were people currently using methamphetamine.

comparison.controls: People with schizophrenia or a related psychotic disorder, intended to be people who did not use drugs. Departures visible in Table 1 and the references: in Hides 2015 the 20 people with a primary psychotic disorder were drawn from 198 people who had used methamphetamine in the previous month; Hajebi 2018 compared first-episode non-affective psychosis (title, p. 189) although first-episode psychosis was an exclusion criterion; Alexander 2019 recruited 39 people with schizophrenia and stimulant dependence besides the 18 without, and the interval widths in Figs. 1 and 2 correspond to about 39 people per group (editors' calculation). The most heavily weighted study (Srisurapanont 2011; 30.4% of the positive-symptom pool and 13.9% of the negative, Figs. 1 and 2) drew its two groups from two different studies, the WHO multi-site project on methamphetamine psychosis and a Thai trial of long-acting injectable risperidone in schizophrenia (Table 1, p. 186): a comparison between groups recruited for different purposes, not a direct comparison.
comparison.matching: None at review level; within studies, mostly unmatched clinical groups.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Premorbid functioning, family history, duration of illness and duration of antipsychotic treatment are not synthesized; antipsychotic dose is reported for six studies (Table 1) and not analysed, although antipsychotics can cause secondary negative symptoms.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Intended to be none; not met in at least one study (Hides 2015) and unreported in others.

outcomes.instruments: PANSS (6 studies), BPRS (5), Manchester scale (1); depressive symptoms by PANSS, BPRS, CDSS or HDRS items (6 studies) (3.2).
outcomes.operationalization: Positive- and negative-symptom severity as baseline or single-time scores, standardized as Hedges' g, methamphetamine psychosis minus schizophrenia (negative values mean fewer symptoms in methamphetamine psychosis) (2.2; 2.7).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Two primary outcomes (positive, negative), depressive symptoms and two negative-symptom dimensions (diminished expression, amotivation), plus sensitivity, leave-one-out and meta-regression analyses.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable at review level; not reported for the included studies.

analysis.effect_sizes: Negative symptoms: SMD -0.35 (95% CI -0.54 to -0.16), 12 studies, I2 54% (tau2 0.057 in Fig. 2); studies with Newcastle-Ottawa scores above 5: -0.44 (-0.82 to -0.07); leave-one-out as reported (the study left out is not named), -0.254 (-0.37 to -0.13), I2 58.0%. Positive symptoms: -0.01 (-0.13 to 0.11), I2 0%, heterogeneity p = 1.00 (Fig. 1). Depressive symptoms (6 studies): -0.01 (-0.41 to 0.39), I2 83%; without one outlier -0.16 (-0.36 to 0.04). Negative-symptom dimensions (3 studies): not significant. Editors' recalculation (Hedges' g, DerSimonian-Laird) from the Table 1 means and dispersions, reading those of Dawe 2011 and Hajebi 2018 as standard errors: positive symptoms -0.29 (-0.67 to 0.10), I2 89%; negative symptoms -0.44 (-0.72 to -0.16), I2 79%; from the Fig. 2 study values, -0.35 (-0.54 to -0.16), I2 54%, as reported, and without Mikami 2003 -0.28 (-0.44 to -0.12), I2 30% (common-effect model: -0.25, -0.38 to -0.13).
analysis.covariates: None; unadjusted group means. Meta-regression on publication year and mean age was not significant for either outcome (3.6).
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42021286619. The text dates the protocol to 14 July 2020, while the registration number carries the year 2021; the registry record was not read. Departures from the stated eligibility criteria (comparison groups using methamphetamine, a first-episode comparison group) are not acknowledged.
analysis.selective_reporting: All stated outcomes are reported; the Newcastle-Ottawa scores and the number of studies in the sensitivity analysis appear only in supplements.
analysis.power: Not addressed; 12 small studies with 14 to 169 people per group (Table 1).

interpretation_gap.results_show: A small-to-moderate average difference in negative-symptom scores (SMD -0.35) between treated, mostly stable groups with methamphetamine psychosis and with schizophrenia, with moderate heterogeneity and 5 of 12 studies individually significant; for positive symptoms a reported null with near-perfect agreement across studies, which the paper's own Table 1 does not reproduce (editors' recalculation -0.29, -0.67 to 0.10, I2 89%, reading two studies' printed dispersions as standard errors; -0.35, -0.90 to 0.20, I2 94%, taking them as printed).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The results conclude that "there are no differences regarding positive symptoms" (p. 184) and the conclusions speak of similar levels of positive symptoms (p. 189): a non-significant difference read as similarity, on a pooled result that cannot be reproduced from Table 1. The abstract's p values (p = 1, p = 0.01) are the heterogeneity tests of Figs. 1 and 2, not tests of the pooled differences; the abstract calls the samples stable outpatients, though five studies included inpatients and only five specified stability; and the discussion's neurobiological accounts (self-medication, sensitization, a continuum of vulnerability) go beyond cross-sectional symptom scores, although they are labelled as hypotheses.

timeline.event: Srisurapanont et al. (2011): 168 people with methamphetamine psychosis from the WHO multi-site project compared with 169 people with schizophrenia from a Thai trial of long-acting injectable risperidone (Table 1, p. 186); the largest included study and the one weighted most heavily in both pools (30.4% of the positive-symptom pool, 13.9% of the negative).
Chen et al. (2015) and Wang et al. (2016a), by the same seven Taiwanese authors, enter both pools with near-identical groups and values (reporting issue 5).
Narrative review of 12 direct comparisons (Wearne & Cornish, 2018), sharing at least three primary studies with this meta-analysis (Chen 2015, Srisurapanont 2011, Wang 2016).
Systematic review of the symptom profile, cited here for the rarity of negative symptoms (Voce et al., 2019).
This meta-analysis, the first systematic meta-analytic comparison of these symptoms by the authors' account (p. 189).
Meta-analysis of cognition in substance-induced psychotic disorders versus schizophrenia-spectrum disorders (Semancikova et al., 2026); identified by the currency check of 2026-10-16, not read.

replication.where_it_stands: The only meta-analysis of symptom severity in methamphetamine psychosis versus schizophrenia. The negative-symptom difference is reproducible from the review's own data (direction robust, size uncertain) and was measured in treated patients; the positive-symptom null is not reproducible as reported and should be cited as a non-significant, imprecise difference, not as similarity. Because it shares primary studies with the 2018 narrative review, the two are not independent support.

funding.declared_conflicts: S. Kaiser has received royalties from Boehringer Ingelheim; all other authors declare no conflict of interest (p. 189).
funding.affiliations_note: Faculty of Medicine, University of Geneva, and Division of Adult Psychiatry, Geneva University Hospitals; none of the authors is an author of an included study (references, pp. 189–190).

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study enrolling people at first presentation with psychosis after recent methamphetamine use, with verified abstinence, blinded ratings of positive and negative symptoms at presentation and at 1, 6 and 12 months, and a first-episode schizophrenia comparison group without drug use matched for antipsychotic exposure, analysing resolving and persistent cases separately and testing how well symptom profiles predict the later diagnosis.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population, comparison group, outcomes and designs are specified (2.2, 2.4).

Registered in PROSPERO (2.1); the registry record was not read, the year implied by the number (2021) does not match the stated date (14 July 2020), and departures from the stated eligibility criteria are not acknowledged.
The restriction to observational designs is stated (2.4) but not explained; only observational designs can compare diagnostic groups, so this is a strict reading of a non-critical item.

Three databases to 16 December 2022 with search terms given and reference-list snowballing (2.3); but English-language, human and adult-age limits were applied without any justification, and AMSTAR 2 gives 'partial yes' only when such publication restrictions are justified, so the item is not met. No grey literature or registries were searched either.
Three authors independently inspected titles, abstracts and methods (2.3, 2.5).

The extraction description (2.5) lists study characteristics and says disagreements were resolved by consensus, but does not say who extracted the symptom scores or whether in duplicate; the mismatches between Table 1 and the forest plots (reporting issues 1 to 4) indicate the extracted values were not cross-checked.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Reasons for exclusion are given only in a supplementary flow chart (2.5; 3.1) and two excluded studies are named in the text; no list of excluded full texts with reasons is described.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives design, key inclusion criteria, diagnostic criteria, group sizes, sex, age, baseline scores and antipsychotic dose; drug use, abstinence and dependence are only in supplements (S2, S3) not read.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Two authors independently applied a modified Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (2.6), which covers selection, comparability and ascertainment but not selection of the reported result; study scores are only in a supplement.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: Random-effects pooling of Hedges' g is appropriate in principle, but unadjusted group means were pooled without justification across acute and persistent psychosis and across comparison groups that did not meet the review's own criteria; two included studies probably share participants; and the positive-symptom study estimates in Fig. 1 cannot be reproduced from the extracted means in Table 1, so the pooled positive-symptom result cannot be verified (reporting issue 1). Judged not met. The leave-one-out estimate also appears to come from a common-effect model although random effects are stated for every analysis (key finding 2). With items 4 and 7 also not met, the overall rating would stay critically low even if this item were met.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Sensitivity analysis restricted to studies with Newcastle-Ottawa scores above 5 (3.5).

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The limitations name the heterogeneity of populations, polysubstance use, unreported abstinence and medication and the cross-sectional design (4.6), and the quality-restricted sensitivity analysis is reported.
I2 reported, leave-one-out and meta-regression on year and age performed, and sources of heterogeneity discussed (3.3.2, 3.6, 4.6).
Funnel plots for both outcomes and Egger's test for negative symptoms (t = -1.09, df = 10, p = 0.303) (3.3); with 12 studies the test has little power.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Internal funding and one author's royalties are declared (p. 189).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Three critical items are not met (4: English-language, human and age limits without justification; 7: no list of excluded studies; 11: pooled positive-symptom values that the review's own table does not reproduce, unadjusted means pooled across mixed and partly ineligible groups, and probable double counting of one sample), with items 2 and 9 only partly met: critically low confidence. Items 4 and 11 alone give this rating, so it does not depend on item 7, which was judged from the article's description of a supplementary flow chart that was not read. The negative-symptom estimate is reproducible from the review's data and may be cited as a small-to-moderate difference in treated patients, with these caveats; the positive-symptom result may be cited only as a non-significant and imprecise difference.

key_findings.finding: From 2052 records (PubMed, Embase, PsycINFO to 16 December 2022), 12 studies were included: 624 people with methamphetamine-induced psychosis and 527 with schizophrenia or a related disorder; designs given as 6 cross-sectional (two with a case-control design), 3 case-control, 2 cohort and 1 prospective study.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (p. 182); 2.3 (p. 183); 3.1 Literature search and 3.2, 1st paragraph (p. 184); Table 1 (pp. 185–186)
key_findings.note: The abstract gives 524 people with schizophrenia; the results text and Table 1 give 527.

key_findings.finding: Negative symptoms were less severe in methamphetamine psychosis: SMD -0.35 (95% CI -0.54 to -0.16), 12 studies, I2 54%. Five of the 12 study intervals exclude no difference (Mikami 2003 -1.05, Hajebi -0.68, Dawe -0.41, Chen -0.41, Wang -0.41); two point estimates are zero or above (Howells 0.00, Alexander 0.17).
key_findings.note: Study values read from Fig. 2, an image, which labels Hajebi as 2016 (2018 in Table 1 and the references).

key_findings.finding: Robustness of the negative-symptom result: restricted to studies with Newcastle-Ottawa scores above 5, SMD -0.44 (-0.82 to -0.07, p = 0.04), positive symptoms unchanged; a leave-one-out analysis for potential outliers (the funnel plot flagged Mikami 2003) gave -0.254 (-0.37 to -0.13) with I2 58.0%, without naming the study left out; Egger's test t = -1.09, df = 10, p = 0.303.
key_findings.note: The number of studies in the sensitivity analysis is not given in the text. Editors' recalculation from the Fig. 2 values, reproduced by the second reader: omitting Mikami 2003 gives -0.28 (-0.44 to -0.12), I2 30%, with random effects (DerSimonian-Laird) and -0.25 (-0.38 to -0.13) with a common-effect model, which matches the printed estimate; the printed I2 of 58.0% matches omitting one of several other single studies (for example Zhang 2018), not Mikami. The printed result therefore looks like a common-effect leave-one-out, although 2.7 states random effects for every analysis.

key_findings.finding: Positive symptoms did not differ significantly: SMD -0.01 (-0.13 to 0.11); Fig. 1 shows I2 0%, tau2 0 and a heterogeneity p of 1.00, with all 12 study values between -0.19 and 0.15.
key_findings.note: These study values cannot be reproduced from Table 1 (reporting issue 1).

key_findings.finding: Editors' recalculation from Table 1 (Hedges' g, DerSimonian-Laird random effects; the dispersions printed for Dawe 2011 and Hajebi 2018 treated as standard errors, as their negative-symptom values in Fig. 2 require): positive symptoms -0.29 (-0.67 to 0.10), I2 89%, with study values from -1.93 (Mikami 2003) and -1.11 (Alexander 2019) to 0.54 (Srisurapanont 2011); negative symptoms -0.44 (-0.72 to -0.16), I2 79%, with 11 of the 12 study values in Fig. 2 reproduced (Mikami 2003: about -2.1 from Table 1, -1.05 in Fig. 2).
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation, recomputed by the second reader (AI reader 15) and by the adjudicator, with the same results. Taking every Table 1 dispersion as an SD, as printed: positive symptoms -0.35 (-0.90 to 0.20), I2 94%, study values from -1.98 to 1.20; negative symptoms -0.99 (-1.66 to -0.33), I2 96%.

key_findings.finding: Depressive symptoms (6 studies) did not differ: SMD -0.01 (-0.41 to 0.39), I2 83%; without the outlying study (Srisurapanont 2011) -0.16 (-0.36 to 0.04, p = 0.08). Diminished expression and amotivation (3 studies) did not differ significantly.

Samples departed from the stated criteria: Hides 2015's primary psychotic disorder group (20) came from 198 people who had used methamphetamine in the previous month; Hajebi 2018's comparison group had first-episode non-affective psychosis although first-episode psychosis was an exclusion criterion; five studies included inpatients although the abstract describes stable outpatients; only five specified a period of clinical stability; only one specified that methamphetamine was the main drug; six reported other substance use.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (p. 182); 2.4 Eligibility criteria (p. 183); 3.2, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 184); Table 1, Hides and Hajebi rows (p. 185)
key_findings.note: Hajebi's comparison group is identified from the reference title (p. 189). Its baseline PANSS positive means (31.9 and 33.4; Table 1) are those of acutely ill people, consistent with a first-episode cohort assessed at admission rather than with stable outpatients (editors' inference).

key_findings.finding: Chen 2015 and Wang 2016a, by the same seven Taiwanese authors, report near-identical groups and values: 56 vs 54 and 53 vs 53 people; negative symptoms 9.0 vs 10.5 and 9.1 vs 10.6; positive symptoms 17.0 vs 18.2 and 16.8 vs 18.2; mean antipsychotic doses 1100 ± 600 vs 1200 ± 600 mg/day chlorpromazine equivalents in both; both enter every pool.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, rows Chen et al., 2015 and Wang et al., 2016a (pp. 185–186); references (pp. 189–190)
key_findings.note: Editors' inference: probably overlapping samples, so one sample may be counted twice; the review does not discuss it.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the cross-sectional design of the included studies allows no causal interpretation, that participants with methamphetamine psychosis also used other substances, and that abstinence, methamphetamine dose, severity of dependence and current medication were heterogeneous or unreported.

reporting_issues.issue: The 12 study SMDs for positive symptoms in Fig. 1 (-0.19 to 0.15; I2 0%) cannot be reproduced from the means and dispersions in Table 1. Reading the dispersions printed for Dawe 2011 and Hajebi 2018 as standard errors (reporting issue 2), Table 1 implies study values from -1.93 to 0.54 and a pooled -0.29 (-0.67 to 0.10) with I2 89%; taking every dispersion as an SD, as printed, study values from -1.98 to 1.20 and a pooled -0.35 (-0.90 to 0.20) with I2 94% (editors' recalculations, reproduced by the second reader). Either way none of the Fig. 1 values is reproduced; for example Mikami 2003, 1.7 ± 2.1 vs 7.3 ± 3.8, appears in Fig. 1 as -0.04. The Fig. 1 values themselves pool to the reported -0.01 (-0.13 to 0.11), I2 0%, so the fault lies in the study-level inputs, not in the pooling.
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline positive-symptom result (-0.01, -0.13 to 0.11) cannot be verified; either Table 1 or the analysis input is wrong. It should not be cited as evidence that positive symptoms are similar.

reporting_issues.issue: Mikami 2003's negative-symptom values in Table 1 (1.4 ± 2.3 vs 7.5 ± 3.6) imply an SMD of about -2.1, while Fig. 2 shows -1.05.
reporting_issues.consequence: With the value in Table 1 the pooled negative-symptom estimate would be about -0.44 instead of -0.35 (editors' recalculation); the direction is unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: The dispersions printed for Dawe 2011 (0.52 to 1.07) and Hajebi 2018 (0.7 to 0.9) in Table 1, headed mean ± SD, behave as standard errors: only as standard errors do they reproduce these studies' negative-symptom SMDs in Fig. 2 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers computing effects from Table 1 would get grossly inflated values for these two studies.

reporting_issues.issue: The interval widths in Figs. 1 and 2 match the group sizes in Table 1 for 9 studies but correspond to about 39 vs 39 people for Alexander 2019 (Table 1: 39 vs 18), 20 vs 20 for Hides 2015 (81 vs 20) and 28 vs 28 for Howells 2018 (24 vs 28) (editors' calculation from the printed intervals).
reporting_issues.consequence: The analysis appears to have used group sizes, and for Alexander 2019 possibly the comparison group with stimulant dependence, other than those in Table 1.

reporting_issues.issue: Chen 2015 and Wang 2016a share all seven authors and report near-identical group sizes, symptom scores and identical antipsychotic doses (Table 1).
reporting_issues.consequence: Probable double counting of one Taiwanese sample in every pool (editors' inference), which narrows the intervals and adds a duplicated weight to the negative-symptom difference.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's p values for the pooled effects (p = 1 for positive, p = 0.01 for negative symptoms) are the heterogeneity-test p values printed in Figs. 1 and 2; from the printed intervals the pooled differences would have p of about 0.87 and 0.0003 (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Does not change direction; indicates that output was transcribed without checking.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives 524 people with schizophrenia (results and Table 1: 527), and its design counts (6 cross-sectional, 3 case-control, 2 cohort) sum to 11 of the 12 studies.
The PROSPERO number CRD42021286619 carries the year 2021, while the text dates the protocol's publication to 14 July 2020.
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether registration preceded the work cannot be checked from the article; the registry record was not read.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 3.2 says six studies assessed depression and anxiety but cites eight, including Wang 2016b, the aripiprazole-risperidone trial, which is not an included study; Hajebi is dated 2016 in the forest plots and 2018 in Table 1 and the references; 67.0% men is not a possible proportion of 53 (Wang 2016a, schizophrenia group); Dawe 2011 is described in Table 1 as 98 outpatients while its title describes inpatients.
reporting_issues.consequence: Labelling errors that lower confidence in data handling without changing the estimates.

reporting_issues.issue: The score ranges given in 3.3.1 and 3.3.2 as PANSS ranges (positive 14.5-19.8 for methamphetamine psychosis and 14-19.8 for schizophrenia; negative 7-17 and 8.9-19.8) do not match Table 1: they include values from Dawe 2011, which used the BPRS (19.84, 7.12, 8.98), and leave out Hajebi 2018 (31.9 and 33.4) and Howells 2018 (8 and 12). Section 3.3.1 also says the positive-symptom data came from 12 studies using PANSS positive scores, while 3.2 says 6 used the PANSS, 5 the BPRS and 1 the Manchester scale.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor for the estimates; a further sign that values were transcribed without being checked.

disagreements.first_pass: key_findings[2].finding: leaving out the outlier (Mikami 2003), -0.254 (-0.37 to -0.13) with I2 58.0%;; key_findings[2].note: An editors' DerSimonian-Laird recalculation from the Fig. 2 values without Mikami 2003 gives -0.28 (-0.44 to -0.12) with I2 30%, not the reported I2 of 58%; the leave-one-out method is not described.; analysis.effect_sizes: leaving out the outlier, -0.254 (-0.37 to -0.13), I2 58.0%.; analysis.effect_sizes: and without Mikami 2003 -0.28 (-0.44 to -0.12), I2 30%.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 15: confirmed, with a recalculation: omitting Mikami from the Fig. 2 values gives -0.28 (-0.44; -0.12), I2 30% with random effects, and -0.25 (-0.38; -0.13) with a common-effect model, which matches the printed -0.254 (-0.37 to -0.13); the printed I2 of 58% matches omitting most other single studies (for example Zhang, 58.0%), not Mikami. The note could say so instead of 'the method is not described'.
disagreements.resolution: Recomputed from the twelve Fig. 2 values read at 300 dpi (rendered p. 187): without Mikami, random effects -0.278 (-0.44 to -0.12), I2 30.1%; common effect -0.253 (-0.38 to -0.13); omitting Zhang gives I2 58.0%, Okada 57.9%. The text (3.3.2, 4th paragraph, p. 184) does not name the study left out; the card no longer says it was Mikami. Finding, note and effect-size summary corrected.

disagreements.first_pass: reporting_issues[0].issue: The 12 study SMDs for positive symptoms in Fig. 1 (-0.19 to 0.15; I2 0%) cannot be reproduced from the means and SDs in Table 1, which imply study values from -1.93 to 0.54 and a pooled -0.29 (-0.67 to 0.10) with I2 89% (editors' recalculation); for example Mikami 2003, 1.7 ± 2.1 vs 7.3 ± 3.8, appears in Fig. 1 as -0.04.; key_findings[4].note: Editors' calculation, to be recomputed by the second reader.; analysis.effect_sizes: Editors' recalculation (Hedges' g, DerSimonian-Laird) from the Table 1 means and SDs:; interpretation_gap.results_show: (editors' recalculation -0.29, -0.67 to 0.10, I2 89%).
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 15: corrected: numbers right, assumption missing: the values implied by Table 1 (-1.93 to 0.54; -0.29, -0.67 to 0.10, I2 89%) hold only when the Dawe 2011 and Hajebi 2018 dispersions are read as standard errors; taken as printed, study values -1.98 to 1.20 and -0.35 (-0.90 to 0.20), I2 94%. Either way none of the Fig. 1 values is reproduced, and the Fig. 1 values themselves pool to the reported -0.01, so the fault lies in the study-level inputs.
disagreements.resolution: Recomputed independently from Table 1 (rendered pp. 185–186): with the two studies' dispersions multiplied by the square root of n, -0.29 (-0.67 to 0.10), tau2 0.397, I2 89%, studies -1.93 (Mikami) to 0.54 (Srisurapanont); as printed, -0.35 (-0.90 to 0.20), I2 94%, studies -1.98 (Hajebi) to 1.20 (Dawe); negative symptoms as printed -0.99 (-1.66 to -0.33), I2 96%. Re-pooling the Fig. 1 values gives -0.01 (-0.13 to 0.11), I2 0%. The assumption and the alternative are now stated wherever the recalculation appears; consequence unchanged.

disagreements.first_pass: risk_of_bias.domains[3].judgment: partial-yes; risk_of_bias.domains[3].note: Three databases to 16 December 2022 with search terms given and reference-list snowballing (2.3); English, human and age limits without justification, and no grey literature or registries. 'Partial yes' as in the project's other review cards.; risk_of_bias.domains[10].note: Judged not met; had it been met, the overall rating would be low rather than critically low.; risk_of_bias.reasoning: Two critical items are not met (7: no list of excluded studies; 11: pooled positive-symptom values that the review's own table does not reproduce, unadjusted means pooled across mixed and partly ineligible groups, and probable double counting of one sample), with items 2, 4 and 9 only partly met: critically low confidence.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 15: disagree on item 4, proposed no: English-language, human and age limits are not justified (2.3), and the AMSTAR 2 partial yes requires justified restrictions; overall unchanged. On the overall: item 7 rests partly on a supplementary flow chart not available; if it listed the excluded studies with reasons, item 11 alone would make the overall low confidence.
